shared_context.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that x satisfies the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m, namely: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then N(m,g), the number of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g, is equal to the cardinality of K_{m,g}.

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a numerical semigroup, meaning a subset S of the nonnegative integers that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement. Assume its multiplicity is m, meaning m >= 2 is the least positive element of S. Then there exists a unique tuple x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers with the following property: for each r in {1,...,m-1}, x_r is the least positive integer q such that q m + r belongs to S, and for every nonnegative integer q one has q m + r belongs to S if and only if q >= x_r.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup, and let m\ge 2 be its multiplicity, i.e. the least positive element of S.

We must prove that there exists a unique tuple x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for every r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}:
1. x_r is the least positive integer q with qm+r\in S, and
2. for every q\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}, one has qm+r\in S if and only if q\ge x_r.

We proceed residue class by residue class.

Fix r with 1\le r\le m-1.

First, we show that the set
A_r:=\{q\in \mathbb Z_{>0}: qm+r\in S\}
is nonempty. Since S has finite complement in \mathbb N_0, the set \mathbb N_0\setminus S is finite. But the arithmetic progression
\{r, m+r, 2m+r, 3m+r, \dots\}
contains infinitely many nonnegative integers. Therefore not all of its terms can lie in the finite set \mathbb N_0\setminus S. Hence there exists some integer q\ge 0 such that qm+r\in S.

Now q cannot be 0, because then qm+r=r\in S, but 1\le r<m and m is the least positive element of S, so no positive integer smaller than m belongs to S. Thus q>0. Therefore A_r is nonempty.

Since A_r is a nonempty subset of the positive integers, by well-ordering it has a least element. Define x_r to be that least element. Then x_r\in \mathbb Z_{>0} and
x_r m+r\in S,
with x_r minimal among positive q having this property.

This defines a tuple x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})\in (\mathbb Z_{>0})^{m-1}. So existence of a candidate tuple is established.

Next we prove the threshold property: for every q\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0},
qm+r\in S \iff q\ge x_r.

Proof of "if": assume q\ge x_r. Since x_r m+r\in S and m\in S, and S is closed under addition, we have
qm+r=(x_r m+r)+(q-x_r)m\in S,
because q-x_r\ge 0 and therefore (q-x_r)m\in S (it is a sum of q-x_r copies of m, or 0 if q=x_r).

Proof of "only if": assume qm+r\in S. We must show q\ge x_r. If q=0, then qm+r=r\in S, impossible because 1\le r<m and m is the least positive element of S. Hence q>0. But x_r was defined as the least positive integer q' such that q'm+r\in S. Since q is a positive integer with qm+r\in S, minimality of x_r gives x_r\le q, i.e. q\ge x_r.

Thus for this fixed r,
qm+r\in S \iff q\ge x_r
for all q\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.

Since r was arbitrary in \{1,\dots,m-1\}, the above holds for every residue r, so the tuple x satisfies the required property.

It remains to prove uniqueness. Suppose y=(y_1,\dots,y_{m-1}) is another tuple of positive integers such that for every r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, y_r is the least positive integer q with qm+r\in S, and equivalently satisfies the same threshold property. Fix r. Both x_r and y_r are the least positive integer q such that qm+r\in S. A least element of a given subset of the positive integers is unique, so x_r=y_r. Since this holds for every r=1,\dots,m-1, we conclude x=y.

Therefore there exists exactly one tuple x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that, for each r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, x_r is the least positive integer q with qm+r\in S, and for every q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}, qm+r\in S if and only if q\ge x_r. This is exactly the claim.
result_payload.proof_summary: For each nonzero residue r mod m, finite complement of S implies some number congruent to r mod m lies in S; since no positive integer < m lies in S, the first such occurrence is at qm+r with q>0. Define x_r as the least such q. Closure under addition with m shows all larger q also work, giving qm+r in S iff q>=x_r. Uniqueness follows because each x_r is the unique least element of the same set.
